front:
Name the processes
responsible for the following
phase changes: solid ⇄ gas
back:
Sublimation (s to g)
Deposition (g to s)

front: What is diffusion and in which substances does it occur?
back:
Diffusion is the process where particles spread out, moving from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration (down the concentration gradient).

It occurs in gases and liquids (solutions).

front: What is an element?
back: An element is a substance made up of only one type of atom.

front:
Elements can be classified into
two groups based on their
properties; what are these
groups?
back: Metals and non-metals

front: What is a compound?
back:
Two or more elements combined chemically in fixed proportions which can
be represented by formulae

front:
Do compounds have the
same properties as their
constituent elements?
back: No, they have different properties.

front:
Do mixtures have the
same chemical properties as their constituent materials?
back:
The constituent materials keep their own chemical
properties, but the mixture may have different chemical properties (e.g.
melting point) as a whole.

front:
What are the five methods to separate mixtures?

Do these involve chemical reactions?
back:
• Filtration
  • evaporation/crystallisation
  • simple distillation
  • fractional
  • distillation
  • chromatography

They do not involve chemical reactions

front: Describe and explain fractional distillation
back:
Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids based on their different boiling points

The mixture is heated until it vaporizes and passes into a fractionating column. The column is hot at the bottom and cool at the top - the liquids condense at different heights based on their boiling points.

front:
Describe and explain
filtration
back:
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (within which it is suspended)

The mixture is poured onto filter paper on a funnel. The liquid (filtrate) passes through the filter paper, but the insoluble solid (the residue) is caught as pits articles are too big.

front:
Describe and explain
chromatography
back:
Chromatography separates a mixture of substances dissolved in a solvent based on their movement through a medium.

A piece of paper with a spot containing a mixture is placed in a beaker with some solvent. The bottom of the paper is in contact with the solvent. The solvent level slowly rises, separating the spot (mixture) into few spots (components).

front: In a paper chromatography experiment, a compound A has an Rf value of 0.85 - what does it tell you about the compound?
back: It has a higher affinity for the solvent than for the paper.

front:
Describe the structure of an
atom
back:
The atom has a small central nucleus (made up of protons and neutrons)
around which there are electrons.

front:
State the relative masses and
relative charges of the proton,
neutron and electron
back:
Proton: mass 1, charge 1
Neutron: mass 1, charge 0
Electron: mass 1/2000, charge -1

front:
Atoms of the same element have
the same number of which particle
in the nucleus?
back: Protons

front:
Where is the majority of
mass of an atom?
back: The nucleus

front:
How does one calculate the
number of neutrons using mass
number and atomic number?
back: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number.

front:
What is an isotope? Do isotopes
of a certain element have the same
chemical properties?
back:
Atoms of the same element (same proton number) that have a different
number of neutrons.
They have the same chemical properties as they have the same
electronic structure.

front:
Describe the properties of noble
gases. Discuss the trend in boiling
point down the group.
back:
Non-metals, colourless gases at room temperature, low boiling points,
unreactive (full outer shell; they don’t easily accept or lose electrons).
The boiling point increases down the group, as the atoms get heavier.

front:
The elements of Group 0
are more commonly known
as…?
back: The noble gases

front: What is the difference in electron shell configuration between elements in the same period?
back: Same number of electron shells, but number of electrons in their outermost shell increases from left to right across the period.

front:
What change in shell
number is seen as one
moves down a group?
back: The number of shells increases

front:
Elements that react to form
positive ions are…?
back: Metals

front: Which elements do not typically form positive ions during chemical reactions?
back: Non-metals (they usually gain electrons to form negative ions or share electrons in covalent bonds).

front:
Elements in Group 1 are
known as…?
back: The alkali metals

front:
Elements in Group 7 are
known as…?
back: The halogens

front: What is ionic bonding?
back: Ionic bonding is the transfer of electron(s) from a metal atom to a non-metal atom to form positive and negative ions which are then strongly electrostatically attracted.

front: How are ionic compounds held together?
back: They are held together by electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a giant lattice.

front:
State properties of ionic
substances
back:
High melting and boiling point (strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions).

Do not conduct electricity when solid (ions in fixed positions).

Conduct when molten or dissolved in water - ions are free to move.

front:
How are ionic compounds
formed?
back:
Reaction of a metal with a non-metal.
Electron transfer occurs - metal gives away its outer shell electrons to
non-metal.

front: What is a covalent bond?
back: Covalent bond is the strong electrostatic force of attraction of a shared pair of electrons of two atoms and their nuclei.

front: Describe the structure and properties of simple molecular covalent substances
back:
- Weak intermolecular forces, so low melting and boiling points
- Small molecules
- Do not conduct electricity (no ions)

front:
How do intermolecular forces
change as the mass/size of the
molecule increases? How does this affect boiling/melting points?
back:
They increase. That causes melting/boiling points to increase as well (more
energy needed to overcome these forces)

front:
What are giant covalent
substances? Give properties and examples
back:
Solids, atoms covalently bonded together in a giant lattice.

High melting/boiling points – strong covalent bonds.

Mostly don’t conduct electricity (no delocalised e−)

Diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide (silica).

front: Describe the structure and properties of diamond
back:
– four, strong covalent bonds for each carbon atom
– very hard (Strong bonds)
– very high melting point (strong bonds)
– does not conduct electricity (no delocalised electrons)

front: What is graphite? Explain its properties.
back:
– Giant covalent structure with three covalent bonds for each carbon atom forming layers of hexagonal rings
– layers free to slide as weak intermolecular forces between layers; soft, can be used as a lubricant
– high melting point
– conduct thermal and electricity due to one delocalised electron per each carbon atom

front: Describe and explain the properties of fullerenes and give the most common example
back:
– hollow shaped molecules

– based on carbon 6-rings, some 5/7

– C60 (Buckminsterfullerene)

front:
Describe and explain the
properties of nanotubes
back:
– cylindrical fullerene with high length to diameter ratio
- High tensile strength (strong bonds)
- Conductivity (deloc. electrons)

front: What is graphene
back: A single layer of graphite.

front: What affects the energy needed to change state from solid to liquid or liquid to gas?
back: The strength of forces between particles. Stronger forces mean higher energy, melting, and boiling points.

front:
A pure substance will melt
or boil at…? What about the
mixture?
back:
A fixed temperature.
A mixture will melt over a range of temperatures.

front:
What are the three states of
matter?
back: Solid, liquid and gas

front:
Write a balanced equation
of magnesium reacting with
hydrochloric acid.
back: Mg<sub>(s)</sub> + 2HCl<sub>(aq)</sub> → MgCl<sub>2(aq)</sub> + H<sub>2(g)</sub>

front:
The following reaction occurs in a heated test tube:

4MgO(s) + CH4(g) → 4Mg(s) + 2H2O(g) + CO2(g)

The mass appears to decrease. Why?
back: The carbon dioxide and water escape as they are gases

front:
What is the formula that
links mass, molecular mass
and moles together
back: Mass (g) = Mr x Moles

front: Why is it often not possible to obtain the theoretical yield in a chemical reaction?
back:
Reversibility: The reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible, leading to an equilibrium where both reactants and products are present.

Product Loss: Some of the product may be lost during the process of separation from the reaction mixture

Side Reactions: Some of the reactants might undergo side reactions, producing unintended by-products.

front:
State three characteristics of
the alkali metals
back:
• One electron in their outer shell
  • Low density
  • Very reactive (stored under oil to prevent reactions with oxygen or water)
  • Soft (can be cut with knife).

front:
Describe the product (and its colour) formed by reacting Group 1 elements with non-metals.

Why are these reactions similar for the different Group 1 elements?
back:
The products are soluble white ionic compounds that form colourless solutions.

They all have one electron in their outer shell.

front: How do Group 1 elements react with water? Describe the products.
back:
They react vigorously with water, fizzing and moving around on the surface.

Products: hydrogen gas is released and hydroxides are formed which dissolve to make an alkaline solution

front: State five characteristics of Group 7 (halogens)
back:
- 7 electrons in outer shell
- Coloured vapours
- Mostly diatomic molecules
- Form ionic salts with metals
- Form molecular compounds with non-metals

front: State the first five halogens and their states of matter and colour (at room temperature)
back:
- Fluorine, pale yellow gas.
- Chlorine, pale green gas.
- Bromine, dark brown liquid (orange vapour and solution).
- Iodine, grey solid (gives off purple vapour when heated).

- Astatine, solid

front: State three trends seen down group 7 (halogens)
back:
- Higher atomic mass
- Higher melting and boiling point
- Less reactive (electrons less easily gained)

front:
Write the
equation and state the colour change seen when a bromine solution reacts with a sodium iodide solution.
back: Br2(aq)  + 2NaI(aq) → I2(aq)  + 2NaBr(aq); a brown colour of I2 in solution would appear

front: Name the commonly soluble ionic compounds
back:
All nitrate salts
Common potassium, sodium and ammonium salts
Common sulfate salts - except barium, calcium and lead(II)
Common chloride salts - except silver and lead(II)

[Think: common salt and fertilisers must easily dissolve]

front:
You have a sample of a
pure liquid. What's the simple way to check its identity?
back:
Measure the boiling point.
Say we have water - it boils at 100 Celsius degrees.

front:
How can you show that a
liquid contains pure water? (More tricky than checking boiling point)
back: Add the liquid being tested to a sample of pure, anhydrous crystals of CuSO<sub>4</sub> (white). The positive test will result in the formation of the blue, hydrated copper (II) sulfate.

front: What is the test for ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions?
back: Add a few drops of dilute sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH), then warm gently. Ammonia (NH3) gas is produced if ammonium ions are present. Put damp litmus paper near the end of the test tube - it should turn blue

front:
State the colours of flames
observed when lithium,
sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions burn
in oxygen
back:
Red, Li+
Yellow, Na+
Lilac, K+
Orange-red, Ca2+
Blue-green, Cu2+

front:
What is
oxidation/reduction in terms of oxygen?
back:
Oxidation is the addition of oxygen
Reduction is the loss of oxygen

front:
What is oxidation/reduction in terms of
electron transfer ?
back:
Oxidation – loss of electrons.   OIL
Reduction – gain of electrons.  RIG

front:
What is the general equation for a
reaction between metals and
acids? What type of reaction is
this?
back:
Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen
Redox reaction, also a displacement reaction.

front:
Which metals in the reactivity
series will react with acid? What gas is given off?
back: Those above hydrogen. Hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) is given off.

front:
What is the general equation for a
neutralisation reaction?
back: Acid + Base → Salt + Water

front:
What is the general equation for
the reaction between metal
carbonate and acid?
back: Metal Carbonate + Acid → Salt + Water + Carbon Dioxide

front:
What is the general equation for
the reaction between metal oxide
and acid?
back:
Metal Oxide + Acid → Salt + Water
(Same as alkali + acid)

front: What is a redox reaction?
back: A reaction where both oxidation and reduction occurs

front:
Explain in terms of gain or loss of
electrons which species has been
oxidised and which species has been
reduced when magnesium reacts with
hydrochloric acid
back:
Magnesium has lost electrons and thus has been oxidised (Mg to Mg<sup>2+</sup>)
The hydrogen in HCl has gained electrons and thus has been reduced (H<sup>+</sup> to H<sub>2</sub>)

front:
What do acids and alkalis
produce in aqueous solutions?
back: Acids produce hydrogen ions, alkalis produce hydroxide ions

front:
What is the pH scale and what
does a pH of 7 show?
back: The measure of acidity/alkalinity of a solution; neutral solution.

front:
State the general equation for a
neutralisation reaction in a short,
ionic form.
back:
H<sup>+</sup>
 + OH<sup>−</sup>
 → H<sub>2</sub>O

front: Explain the difference in how strong and weak acids behave when dissolved in water (aqueous solution)
back:
Strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution - it dissociates fully into its ions

Weak acid is only partially ionised - only a fraction of the acid molecules dissociate into ions

front:
What happens to pH as
concentration of H<sup>+</sup>
 increases?
back: It decreases.

front: What is the difference between a concentrated acid and a dilute acid, and how does this compare to strong and weak acids?
back:
A concentrated acid has more moles of acid per unit volume of water, while a dilute acid has fewer.

This differs from acid strength: a strong acid, which fully ionizes in water, typically has a lower pH, whereas a weak acid, which only partially ionizes, has a higher pH at the same concentration.

front:
Name the following salts:
LiNO<sub>3</sub>
, K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
, MgBr<sub>2</sub>
, BaSO<sub>4</sub>
back:
Lithium nitrate
Potassium carbonate
Magnesium bromide
Barium sulfate

front:
Describe the tests for
hydrogen, oxygen, carbon
dioxide and chlorine
back:
Hydrogen – ‘pop’ heard when burning splint placed over the gas.

Oxygen – glowing splint relights.

Carbon dioxide – turns limewater (Ca(OH)2) milky.

Chlorine – bleaches damp litmus paper white.

front: How is sodium hydroxide used to test for copper and iron?
back:
Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate
Iron(II) forms a dirty green precipitate
Iron(III) forms a brown precipitate

front:
Describe the test for
carbonate anions
back:
Add dilute acid, e.g. HCl
Fizzing observed, as CO2 is evolved -> then do limewater test
E.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2

front: Describe the test for sulfate anions
back:
Add a solution containing barium ions - Ba2+ (E.g. BaCl2 solution). If sulfate anions are present, a white precipitate of BaSO4 forms

E.g. K2SO4 + BaCl2 → 2KCl + BaSO4

front: What are the approximate proportions of the top four gases in the modern atmosphere
back:
78% of N2
21% of O2
1% of Argon
0.04% of CO2

front: How have human activities led to an increase in the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane?
back:
Carbon dioxide – combustion of fossil fuels and deforestation.
Methane – increased farming and decomposition in landfills.

front:
Name four potential effects
of global climate change
back:
Any of these:
- Global warming
- Melting of glaciers and polar ice caps; sea level rise, flooding and increased coastal erosion.
- Changes in the amount, timing and distribution of rainfall and storms.
- Temperature and water stress for humans and wildlife.
- Changes in the food-producing capacity of some regions.
- Changes to the distribution of wildlife species.

front: What are two issues regarding sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen?
back:
They cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.

Acid rain kills animals (by making the lakes in which they live in acidic) and damages plants and buildings.

front: Give four examples of exothermic reaction
back: Freezing, condensing, combustion, oxidation, respiration and neutralisation.

front: Give four examples of endothermic reaction
back: Melting, boiling, thermal decomposition and photosynthesis

front: What is activation energy?
back: Minimum amount of energy that particles need to react.

front:
Name three common ways of
measuring rate of reaction
back:
1. Loss in mass of reactants

2. Volume of gas produced

3. Time for a solution to become opaque (precipitation).

front: Describe how to measure the rate of reaction by monitoring mass loss.
back:
Place the reaction flask on a balance. In these reactions (e.g. metal carbonate +
acid) a gas is given off, so record the decrease in mass in time intervals (note
hydrogen is too light). Plot a graph of mass vs time.

front: Describe how to measure the rate of reaction by monitoring the volume of a gas
back:
Connect a gas syringe to a reaction flask and measure the volume of a gas
formed in time intervals. Plot a graph of volume vs time.

front:
Describe how to measure the rate of reaction by monitoring the disappearance
of a cross.
back:
Take a piece of paper and mark a cross (X) on it. Put the reaction flask on this
cross. Mix the reagents, and measure how long it takes for a cloudy mixture to
conceal a cross.

front: How do you determine the rate of reaction at a specific time t from a graph of reactant amount versus time?
back:
Draw a tangent to the curve at the point t. The slope of the tangent line represents the rate of reaction at time t.

A steeper tangent line indicates a faster rate.

front:
State five factors affecting the
rate of a chemical reaction
back:
Concentration of reactants
Pressure of gases (volume)
Surface area
Temperature
Catalysts

front: Describe and explain the effect of increasing concentration on the rate of reaction
back:
- Conc. increases = faster reaction,
- More reactants = more frequent collisions

front: Describe and explain the effect of increasing pressure of a gas on the rate of reaction
back: More gas molecules in the same volume lead to more frequent collisions, increasing the reaction rate. (Similar to increasing concentration)

front:
Describe and explain the effect of increasing surface
area on a reaction
back:
Increasing the surface area of solid reactants (by e.g. cutting into smaller pieces) increases the frequency of
collisions and so increases the rate of reaction

e.g. block of magnesium reacts slower with acid then magnesium powder

front: Describe the effect of changing the concentration of reactant and product on the position of the equilibrium in a reversible reaction
back:
The system is no longer at equilibrium and the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again.

- If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.

- If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.

front:
What is the empirical
formula? How is it related to
molecular formula?
back:
Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of different elements in the compound.
The two are related by some numerical constant.
E.g. the empirical formula for heptene, C7H14, is CH2 . Multiplying the empirical formula by a numerical constant (7) would yield the molecular formula of heptene.

front:
What is a homologous
series?
back:
Series of compounds with same general formula, same functional groups

similar chemical properties
gradual change in physical properties

front: Hydrocarbon combustion: what kind of reaction and possible products.
back:
An exothermic reaction with oxygen, releasing energy.

Products: water and either carbon dioxide or carbon monoxide/carbon. (depending on oxygen availability)

front: Describe the physical properties of alkanes (including the trend with bigger molecules)
back:
- Poor reactivity.
- Boiling points and viscosity increase as molecules get bigger (smallest molecules are gases, then liquids and biggest are solids.)
- Volatility and flammability decrease as molecules get bigger.

front: What is the first step in the fractional distillation of crude oil?
back: Crude oil is heated and vaporized, and the vapor rises up the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top.

front:
What type of reaction is
cracking?
back: Thermal decomposition.

front: How are the products of cracking used in polymerisation?
back: Alkanes and alkenes are used as monomers in polymerisation to form plastics and other products

front: What is the test for alkenes?
back: Add bromine water. Colour change occurs from orange to colourless.

front: Compare the combustion of alkanes and alkenes
back:
Alkanes: Burn with a cleaner flame, producing less soot and primarily forming carbon dioxide and water.

Alkenes: Burn with a smokier flame, often producing more soot due to a lower hydrogen-to-carbon ratio and the presence of double bonds.

front:
What are addition reactions
of alkenes?
back:
When atoms are added across a carbon-carbon double bond, converting it to a single bond. 

(This reaction increases the saturation of the molecule.)

front: Explain what happens to the double bond when alkanes are used to produce polymers?
back: The C=C double bond becomes just a single bond, and the the two carbons make other bonds.

front:
Give 3 examples of addition
polymers and their uses.
back:
Polyethene - plastic bags

Polytetrafluoroethene (PTFE) - teflon surfaces, for use in non-stick kitchenware

Polychloroethene [previously know as PVC] - water pipes

front:
What is the arrangement of
C-H bonds in methane?
back: Tetrahedral

front:
Why are alkanes considered
unreactive?
back:
They exclusively contain relatively strong C-C and C-H bonds; these are quite
difficult to break.

front: How do alkanes undergo halogenation, and what conditions are necessary for this reaction to occur?
back:
The reaction replaces hydrogen atoms with halogen atoms.

UV light is needed to break halogen molecules into free atoms (e.g. Cl2 becomes 2Cl).

For example, making chloromethane from methane: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl

front: What are isomers? How many isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> are there?
back:
Isomers are compounds of the same molecular formula having different structural formulae.

Three:

front: Addition polymerisation requires an additive - what’s its name and role?
back:
An initiator.

It helps one of the C=C bonds to break, starting the process.

front: Define acid
back: Produces hydrogen ions (H<sup>+</sup>) in aqueous solutions (proton donors) and so have a pH range between 0 and 7

front: Define alkali
back: Alkalis are soluble bases that produce hydroxide ions (OH<sup>-</sup>) in aqueous solutions. They have a pH range between 7 and 14.

front: Define base
back:
A substance which reacts with an acid in a neutralisation reaction to form a salt and
water only. Bases are known as proton acceptors.

front: Define climate change
back:
A change in global climate patterns largely caused by the
increase in concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

front: Describe combustion
back: The burning of a substance in oxygen. Exothermic.

front: Define corrosion
back:
The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the
environment, e.g. rusting occurs when iron is exposed to water and oxygen.

front: Define displacement reaction
back: A chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from a compound.

front: Describe the flame test
back:
Qualitative test used to identify metal ions (cations).

Carried out by inserting a nichrome wire loop with the unknown compound on into a flame and observing the colour.

front: Define galvanise
back: A process used to protect against corrosion by coating the metal with a protective layer of zinc.

front: Describe the greenhouse effect
back:
The increase in the temperature of the Earth’s atmosphere due to the
greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trapping infrared radiation emitted from the surface.

front: Define halides
back: The ions formed when halogen atoms gain an electron. E.g. Cl<sup>-</sup>,  Br<sup>-</sup> and I<sup>-</sup>

front: Define indicators and give 3 examples
back:
A substance used to distinguish between acidic and alkaline solutions.

Examples include phenolphthalein, litmus and methyl orange.

front: Define neutralisation
back: The reaction in which an acid and a base (including alkalis) react to form a salt and water.

front: Define pH scale
back:
A measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution ranging from 0 to 14. The pH
can be measured using universal indicator or a pH probe.

front: Define reactivity series
back: A series in which metals are arranged in order of their reactivity. This can be used to predict products from reactions.

front: Define reducing agent
back:
A substance that brings about reduction by losing electrons. The reducing
agent is itself oxidised.

front: Define reduction
back: A reaction involving the loss of oxygen. Reduction is the gain of electrons.

front: What is rust and what causes it?
back: iron oxide which forms on iron when it undergoes oxidation - in the presence of oxygen and water

front: Describe sacrificial protection
back: The protection of a metal (e.g. iron) against corrosion by coating with a more reactive metal (e.g zinc). This creates a physical barrier to oxygen and water, preventing corrosion

front: Define thermal decomposition
back: The breaking down of a compound by heating

front: Define universial indicator
back: A mixture of dyes that changes colour gradually over a range of pH and is used in testing for acids and alkalis.

front: Define atomic nucleus
back:
Positively charged object composed of protons and neutrons at the centre
of every atom with one or more electrons orbiting it.

front: Define atomic number
back: The number of protons in the nucleus.

front: Define conductor
back:
A material that contains charged particles which are free to move to carry
electrical or thermal energy.

front: Describe evaporation/crystallisation (as a separation method)
back:
Evaporation/crystallisation separates dissolved soluble solids from solutions (e.g., salt from water).

Heat the solution until crystals start to form, leave the solution to cool and then filter the formed crystals from the solution as the solvent evaporates.

front: Define electron
back:
Negatively charged subatomic particle which orbits the nucleus at various energy
levels. Very small relative mass (negligible).

front: Define electron shell
back: Different energy levels in atoms, occupied by electrons.

front: Define electrostatic forces
back: The strong forces of attraction or repulsion between charged ions

front: Define empirical formula
back:
The simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element in a
compound.

front: Define gas
back: The state of matter where the particles have the most energy. The particles in a gas are relatively spread out and move randomly in all directions. Intermolecular forces acting between the particles are very weak.

front: Define group
back: A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in the outer shell.

front: What does inert mean?
back: Unreactive.

front: What are intermolecular forces, and what property do they affect?
back:
The forces which exist between molecules.

The strength of the intermolecular forces impact physical properties like boiling/melting point.

front: Define ion
back: An atom or molecule with an electric charge due to the loss or gain of electrons.

front: Describe lattices - what do they form?
back: A repeating regular arrangement of atoms/ions/molecules that occurs in crystals.

front: Define liquid
back:
The state of matter where the particles are arranged randomly and close together.
The particles are able to move past each other. Intermolecular forces act between the particles.

front: Define mass number
back: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

front: Define metals
back:
Elements that react to form positive ions. Found to the left and towards the bottom of
the periodic table.

front: Define mixture. Comment on their boiling/melting points.
back:
Contains at least two different elements or compounds which are not chemically bonded together.

They may melt or boil over a range of temperatures.

front: Define mobile phase
back:
The fluid (gas or liquid) which moves through the chromatography system,
carrying the mixture which is to be separated.

front: Define mole
back:
Standard unit for measuring amounts of chemicals. The mole is the unit for amount of
substance. The symbol for the unit mole is mol.

front: Define molecular formula
back: The actual ratio of atoms of each element present in a compound.

front: Define molecule
back: A group of at least two atoms held together by covalent bonds.

front: Describe noble gases
back:
The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table. They have a stable full outer
shell of electrons which makes them very unreactive.

front: Define neutron
back: Neutral subatomic particle present in the nucleus of the atom. Relative mass of 1.

front: Define non-metals
back:
Elements that react to form negative ions. Found towards the right and top of
the periodic table.

front: Define percentage yield
back: The percentage ratio of the actual yield of product from a reaction compared with the theoretical yield.

front: Define period with reference to electron shells
back: A row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.

front: What is the periodic table?
back:
Table of elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number and such
that elements with similar properties are in the same column (group).

front: Define proton
back:
Positively charged subatomic particle present in the nucleus of the atom. Relative
mass of 1.

front: Define pure substance
back: A substance which contains only one compound or element and so has fixed melting and boiling points.

front: Define relative atomic mass
back:
An average value that takes account of the abundance of the
isotopes of the element.

front: Define relative formula mass.
back:
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers
shown in the formula

front: Define saturated solution
back:
A solution which contains the maximum amount of solute that can be
dissolved in the solvent. If any more solute is added, it will not dissolve in the solution.

front: Describe simple distillation
back:
A separation technique used to separate a liquid from a solution.

The solution is heated so that only the liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates. This gas is then condensed in a condenser before being collected as a liquid.

front: Define solid
back:
The state of matter where the particles hold a regular arrangement and have the least
amount of energy. They are tightly packed together and can only vibrate about their fixed positions. Strong intermolecular forces act between the particles

front: Define solute
back: A substance which is dissolved in a solvent to create a solution.

front: Define solution
back: A homogeneous mixture in which a solute is dissolved in a solvent.

front: Define solvent
back: A substance which dissolves a solute.

front: Define state symbols
back:
The symbols used in chemical equations to denote the states of the
chemicals reacting: (s) - solid, (l) - liquid, (g) - gas, (aq) - aqueous solution.

front: Define stationary phase
back:
The nonmoving phase which the mobile phase passes over during
chromatography.

front: Define subatomic particles
back:
Particles smaller than an atom. Protons, neutrons and electrons are
the three most common subatomic particles.

front: Define water crystalisation
back: Water molecules forming part of a crystal structure.

front: Define activation energy
back: The minimum amount of energy that particles must collide with to react.

front: Define calorimetry
back:
The process used to measure the amount of heat energy released or absorbed
during a chemical reaction.

front: Define catalyst
back:
Increases the rate of reaction by providing a different reaction pathway with a lower
activation energy. They are not used up during the reaction.

front: According to collision theory, what is required for a reaction to happen?
back:
Chemical reactions only occur when colliding particles collide with the
correct orientation and with sufficient energy (activation energy).

front: Define effect of surface area on reaction rate
back:
Increasing the surface area of the reactants means
there are more exposed reacting particles. This means there are more frequent successful
collisions, so the rate of reaction increases.

front: Define effect of temperature on reaction rate
back:
Increasing the temperature means the particles will
have more kinetic energy and so will move faster. If the molecules are moving faster they will
collide more often and, since they’ve gained kinetic energy, a larger proportion of the
particles will have at least the activation energy. For both these reasons the rate of reaction
increases.

front: Define endothermic reaction
back:
A reaction in which energy is taken in from the surroundings so the
temperature of the surroundings decreases.

front: Define enthalpy change
back: The amount of heat energy given out or absorbed during a reaction.

front: Define exothermic reaction
back:
A reaction in which energy is transferred to the surroundings so the
temperature of the surroundings increases.

front: Define molar enthalpy change
back:
The amount of heat energy given out or absorbed by one mole of a
substance during a reaction. It can be calculated from heat energy change, Q, by dividing Q
by the amount of moles of the substance which took part in the reaction. The value is made
negative if the reaction was exothermic.

front: Define rate of reaction (including units)
back:
The measure of the amount of product formed or reactant used over time.
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s, cm<sup>3</sup>/s or mol/s.

front: Define reversible reaction
back:
A reaction in which the products can react together to reform the
reactants. Reversible reactions are denoted by the symbol ⇌.

front: Define addition polymerisation
back:
The reaction in which many small molecule monomers bond
together to form a long chain polymer.

front: Define addition reaction
back:
A reaction in which at least two molecules combine together to form a
single larger product.

front: Define alkanes, including the general formula
back:
The most common hydrocarbon found in crude oil. Alkanes have the general
formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>.

front: Define alkenes, including the general formula
back:
Hydrocarbons with a double bond between two of the carbon atoms in their chain (C=C),
causing them to be unsaturated. They have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>.

front: Define biodegradable
back: Able to be broken down by living organisms.

front: What is catalytic cracking (incl conditions)
back: Long-chain hydrocarbons are heated to 600-700°C, turning to gas. The vapor passes over a catalyst, splitting the molecules.

front: Define complete combustion
back:
Combustion carried out in sufficient oxygen. Water and carbon
dioxide are the only products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.

front: Define cracking
back:
A process that involves breaking down larger hydrocarbons to produce smaller
more useful molecules.

front: Define crude oil
back:
A finite resource found in rocks. It is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting
mainly of plankton that was buried in mud. Most of the compounds in crude oil are
hydrocarbons.

front: Define displayed formula
back:
A type of structural formula that shows all the bonds between every
atom in the compound.

front: Define finite resource
back: A resource which will one day run out, e.g. crude oil.

front: Define fuel
back: A substance which releases energy when burned

front: Define general formula
back:
A chemical formula which applies to a class of compounds, representing
the composition of the atoms present in the compound. For example, alkanes have the
general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, where n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

front: Define hydrocarbons
back: Compounds made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

front: What are impurities? Give an example of an issue with combustion.
back:
Substances within a compound different to compound itself.
E.g. combustion of hydrocarbons continuing sulfur impurities leads to the formation of sulfur dioxide.

front: Define incomplete combustion
back:
Combustion which is carried out with insufficient oxygen. It can
lead to the production of toxic carbon monoxide and carbon particulates.

front: Define isomerism
back:
The existence of molecules with exactly the same molecular formula but a
different arrangement of atoms in space

front: Define monomer
back: Small short chain molecules which can join together to form a long chain polymer.

front: What do particulates come from and why are they bad?
back:
Carbon particulates (soot) are a product of incomplete combustion. They cause global dimming and health problems for
humans.

front: Define polymer
back: Large long-chain molecules made up of lots of small monomers joined together by covalent bonds.

front: Define saturated hydrocarbons
back:
A hydrocarbon compound containing only single bonds between
carbon atoms. Alkanes are saturated compounds.

front: Define structural formula
back:
A formula which shows the arrangement of atoms in the molecule of a
compound but does not show all the bonds between them. E.g. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>.

front: Define substitution reaction
back:
A reaction in which a functional group of a compound is replaced by
another functional group.

front: Define unsaturated compounds
back:
A compound that contains double or triple carbon bonds so
that it does not contain the maximum number of hydrogen atoms. Alkenes are unsaturated
compounds.

front: What is the formula for R<sub>f</sub>?
What is the general formula for the reaction between a metal and water?
What are the colours for litmus paper?
What are the colours for phenolpthalein?
What are the colours of methyl orange?
back: Orange in neutral

front: How do you test for halides?
What are refinery gases used for?
back: Domestic heating and cooking

front: What is gasoline used for?
back: Fuel in cars

front: What is kerosene used for?
back: Fuel in aircraft

front: What is diesel used for?
back: Fuel in some cars, larger vehicles and trains

front: What is fuel oil used for?
back: Fuel for large ships and some power stations

front: What is bitumen used for?
back: To surface roads and roofs

front: What is the general formula for the combustion of a hydrocarbon?
Write the equation and state the colour change seen when a chlorine solution reacts with a sodium bromide solution.
back:
Cl2(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → Br2(aq)  + 2NaCl(aq)

in this reaction, an orange colour of Br2 in solution would appear

front: Name the commonly insoluble ionic compounds
back:
Common carbonates - all insoluble, except potassium, sodium and ammonium

Common hydroxides - all insoluble, except potassium, sodium and calcium

front: How are hydrocarbons separated during fractional distillation?
back:
Hydrocarbons cool and condense at different heights in the column based on their boiling points.

Large molecules with high boiling points condense at the bottom, while small molecules with low boiling points condense at the top.

front: Draw the displayed formula for the reaction of ethene (C2H4) with bromine (Br2).
back: The reaction results in the addition of bromine atoms across the double bond, producing a compound where each of the original carbon atoms in the double bond now has a bromine atom attached.

front: What is the relationship between alkalis and bases?
back:
Alkalis are a subset of bases that are soluble in water.

All alkalis are bases. Not all bases are alkalis.

front: What is physical chemistry?
back: The study of how substances react, focusing on energy, rates of reaction, and molecular interactions

front: What is organic chemistry?
back: The study of carbon-containing compounds and their reactions.

front: What is inorganic chemistry?
back: The study of non-carbon compounds, including metals and salts.

front: What does soluble mean?
back: A substance is soluble if it can be dissolved in a solvent, e.g. salt in water. An insoluble substance won’t dissolve in a particular solvent.

front: What is the link between relative formula mass and moles
back: Relative formula mass of a substance is numerically equal to the mass of one mole of the substance in grams
